name: Restaurant Brands International Inc.

profile.description: Restaurant Brands International is a quick-service restaurant company that owns and franchises four iconic brands: Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen, and Firehouse Subs. The company operates over 30,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries, primarily through a franchise model. Controlled by 3G Capital. CEO Josh Kobza targets 40,000 restaurants and $60B system-wide sales by 2028.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): RBI has grown through acquisitions (Tim Hortons 2014, Popeyes 2017, Firehouse Subs 2022) rather than organic product innovation. The $400M+ Burger King 'Reclaim the Flame' turnaround plan delivered strong Q1 2026 U.S. same-store sales improvement, but this is brand renovation, not innovation [1]. AI Deployment (1/2): RBI is deploying AI to unify operations — connecting digital ordering, kitchen automation, and supply chain data into a continuous feedback loop across brands [3]. Self-ordering kiosks and predictive ordering are shipping but AI revenue impact is not separately quantified. Market Share (1/2): Burger King is #2 globally in hamburger QSR; Tim Hortons dominates Canadian coffee; Popeyes is top-3 in chicken. Q1 2026 system-wide sales reached $11.51B (+6.2% constant currency), though Popeyes U.S. comp sales fell 6.5% [1]. Pipeline (1/2): RBI targets 5%+ net restaurant growth, 8%+ organic adjusted operating income growth through 2028, with specific milestones of 40,000 restaurants and $60B system-wide sales [1]. R&D Intensity (1/1): Technology investment under CTO Asher Perlmutter and digital transformation across all four brands is above average for the QSR industry [3].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): RBI's corporate purpose is not prominently articulated beyond being 'one of the world's largest quick service restaurant companies.' The individual brands carry strong consumer identity (Tim Hortons = Canadian culture, Burger King = flame-grilled), but RBI corporate lacks a distinctive purpose statement beyond growth and franchise excellence [4]. Community Impact (1/2): Tim Hortons Foundation Camps for underserved youth and Burger King Foundation scholarships represent meaningful but standard corporate philanthropy [4]. ESG metrics are linked to executive compensation including packaging, green building design, and deforestation policies [4]. Employee Retention (1/2): CEO Josh Kobza provides stable leadership since 2023 after ascending internally from CTO to COO to CEO, demonstrating career development culture. However, Glassdoor rating of 3.2/5 with only 49% recommending and complaints about 'non-stop pressure' and work-life balance issues suggest mixed retention [3]. Insider Buying (1/2): 3G Capital maintains its controlling stake, signaling ongoing conviction. No specific open-market insider purchases identified, but the stable large-holder base represents neutral insider sentiment.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Liquidity check passes: ~3,500,000 avg vol x $76.50 = $267.8M >> $1M floor. Calculated mechanically from dividend-stock metrics. D/E of 304% scores 0.0 (1x weight) — franchise-model leverage with $15.7B debt reflecting acquisition history [5]. ROE of 24.0% scores 1.0 (1x) — strong capital efficiency [5]. Revenue Growth YoY of 12.2% (FY2025) scores 1.0 (1x) — Q1 2026 grew 7.4% to $2.26B [1]. Revenue Growth 5yr CAGR of ~11% scores 1.0 (1x) — Firehouse acquisition plus organic growth [1]. Forward P/E of 19.1 scores 1.0 (1x) — just below 20 target [5]. Profit Margin of 8.2% scores 0.41 (1x) — reflects supply chain revenue mix at lower margins [5]. Payout Ratio of ~85% scores 0.25 (1x) — improved from 94% as Q1 2026 net income surged to $338M from $159M [1]. Consecutive Years Paid: 11 scores 1.0 (2x) — dividends since 2015. Consecutive Years Growth: 9 scores 0.9 (1x). 5yr Dividend Growth CAGR: ~4.0% scores 0.67 (2x). Weighted sum = 0+1.0+1.0+1.0+1.0+0.41+0.25+2.0+0.9+1.33 = 8.89 / max 12 x 10 = 7.41, rounds to 7.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): QSR restaurants are physical-world operations — AI cannot replace the cooking, serving, and in-store experience that drives 30,000+ restaurant locations [1]. The franchise model creates structural protection as franchisees own physical assets and local customer relationships. Food preparation, real estate management, and supply chain logistics are AI-resistant activities. Drive-thru ordering and kitchen operations see AI augmentation but not displacement [3]. Some exposure to AI-driven delivery platforms that could shift power dynamics away from restaurant brands toward platform aggregators. AI Opportunity (1/1): RBI is actively deploying AI in operations — predictive ordering, digital menu optimization, self-ordering kiosks, digitized drive-thru lanes, and a unified technology platform connecting ordering, kitchen, and supply data generate measurable efficiency gains across its restaurant network [3].

infinite_game.summary: RBI shows mixed infinite game characteristics. The company's brands have endured for decades (Burger King since 1954, Tim Hortons since 1964), suggesting infinite game DNA at the brand level. Under CEO Josh Kobza, RBI has shifted from 3G Capital's aggressive cost-cutting playbook toward investment-led growth — the $400M+ 'Reclaim the Flame' bet on Burger King U.S. is now delivering strong Q1 2026 results, demonstrating courage to invest for the long term. However, the franchise holding company structure, 304% D/E ratio, and high payout ratio reflect finite financial engineering.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): RBI's purpose is implicitly about making iconic quick-service food accessible worldwide, but this is not articulated as a Just Cause [4]. Strategic communications focus on growth targets — 5%+ restaurant growth, 8%+ operating income growth, 40,000 restaurants by 2028 — rather than a vision of a better future [1]. The individual brands have deep consumer emotional resonance, but RBI corporate operates as a financial holding company optimizing a portfolio.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): CEO Kobza's progression from CTO to COO to CEO demonstrates strong internal career development and leadership continuity [3]. The shift away from 3G Capital's zero-based budgeting culture toward brand investment under Kobza signals improved organizational trust. However, Glassdoor's 3.2/5 rating with 49% recommendation rate and complaints about 'non-stop pressure' and 'terrible culture' from some employees indicate the cultural transformation remains incomplete [3].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (1/1): RBI explicitly uses McDonald's and Chick-fil-A as competitive benchmarks that motivate improvement rather than enemies to destroy. The 'Reclaim the Flame' Burger King improvement plan is directly inspired by competitive pressure — management frames the investment as raising Burger King to competitive standards rather than 'beating' McDonald's [1]. Technology investments are similarly framed as closing gaps with digitally advanced competitors.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): RBI has evolved from a single-brand company to a multi-brand QSR platform through sequential acquisitions (Tim Hortons 2014, Popeyes 2017, Firehouse Subs 2022), demonstrating willingness to expand beyond the original Burger King business [1]. The shift from pure cost-cutting to brand investment under Kobza represents meaningful strategic evolution. However, the core franchise model has not fundamentally changed — this is incremental, not transformative adaptation.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (2/2): The $400M+ 'Reclaim the Flame' investment in Burger King U.S. represents a pattern of choosing long-term brand health over short-term earnings extraction — a direct reversal of the 3G Capital cost-cutting playbook that had degraded the brand [1]. Q1 2026 results validate the bet, with strong BK U.S. same-store sales improvement. CEO Kobza's broader strategic shift from zero-based budgeting to operational excellence and brand investment demonstrates willingness to fundamentally change the company's operating philosophy at the expense of near-term margins.

investment_thesis: Restaurant Brands International delivered a strong Q1 2026 with revenue of $2.26B (+7.4% YoY), net income surging to $338M (+113% from $159M), and adjusted EBITDA of $706M (+10%) [1]. System-wide sales reached $11.51B (+6.2% constant currency) with comp sales up 3.2%, driven by especially strong Burger King U.S. performance validating the $400M+ 'Reclaim the Flame' turnaround [1]. FY2025 delivered $9.43B revenue (+12.2% YoY) with ROE of 24% and a 3.40% dividend yield. At 19.1x forward P/E, the stock trades at a reasonable valuation for a global franchise platform targeting 40,000 restaurants and $60B system-wide sales by 2028.
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on excessive leverage and uneven brand performance. D/E of 304% sits at the Infrastructure scoring floor, reflecting $15.7B in acquisition-driven debt that constrains financial flexibility [5]. While the payout ratio has improved to ~85% with Q1 2026's earnings surge, it remains elevated and leaves limited dividend cushion if earnings decline. Popeyes U.S. same-store sales fell 6.5% in Q1 2026, demonstrating the multi-brand portfolio's uneven execution [1]. Profit margin of 8.2% is thin for a franchise model and reflects the company's supply chain revenue mix. Deforestation-linked supply chain controversies (beef, soy, palm oil) have attracted shareholder activism, and Sustainalytics flagged weak ESG disclosure despite management linking ESG metrics to executive compensation [4]. The 3G Capital ownership overhang creates governance concerns about balancing cost discipline with the brand investment needed for long-term health.
key_catalysts: Burger King U.S. 'Reclaim the Flame' turnaround delivering sustained same-store sales improvement and market share recovery, validated by strong Q1 2026 performance [1]
International expansion driving 5%+ net restaurant growth toward 40,000 restaurants by 2028, with system-wide sales growing 6.2% in Q1 2026 [1]
Earnings inflection — Q1 2026 net income of $338M (+113% YoY) could reset payout ratio and enable accelerated dividend growth and share buybacks [1]
key_risks: Excessive leverage — D/E of 304% at the scoring floor with $15.7B debt constraining financial flexibility and creating vulnerability to rising interest rates [5]
Popeyes U.S. comp sales decline of 6.5% in Q1 2026 indicates uneven brand execution — the turnaround playbook that worked for Burger King may not transfer [1]
Supply chain ESG risk — shareholder resolutions demanding deforestation reporting, weak Sustainalytics disclosure rating, and reputational exposure from beef/soy/palm oil sourcing [4]
